Father of Mercies
FAH-thuhr uhv MUR-seez
divine title
From Latin pater (father) and misericordia (mercy, compassion); the title renders Paul's Greek patēr tōn oiktirmōn, naming God as the source and fountain of all compassion.

Biblical Definition

"Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort." This is Paul's great doxology, and in it he names God by a title that opens the very fountainhead of compassion. To call God the Father of mercies is to say that He is the source, the parent, the begetter of every mercy that has ever fallen upon a sinful world—not one mercy comes but from His hand, and He is rich in mercy without measure. The plural, "mercies," gathers up the manifold and tender compassions of God, His oiktirmoi, the yearning of the bowels of divine pity toward the afflicted. He is likewise "the God of all comfort," who comforts us in all our tribulation that we may be able to comfort others. This title shines brightest against the backdrop of judgment, for the same God who is most holy is also most merciful, and these perfections meet without contradiction in the cross of Christ, where mercy and truth embrace. The mercies of the Father are no fickle moods but the steady overflow of His covenant love, ever near to the broken-hearted. The 1689 Confession confesses Him "most loving, gracious, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in goodness." To the trembling and the comfortless, this name is a refuge: the throne of grace is the seat of the Father of mercies, and they that come find compassion that never runs dry.

Webster 1828 Definition

A title of God expressing that He is the source and fountain of all compassion and tender pity; the God of all comfort.

FATHER OF MERCIES, title. From Latin pater, father, and misericordia, mercy; the scriptural name of God as the source of all compassion.

A title ascribing to God the origin and abundance of all mercy, as a father is the source of his offspring.

Expressing the tender, manifold compassions of God toward the afflicted and the penitent.

Paul's doxology: "the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort" (2Co 1:3).

Denoting that mercy flows from God not by chance but by His very nature and fatherly disposition.

Key Scripture

2Co 1:3 — "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort."

Eph 2:4 — "But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us."

Psa 103:13 — "Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him."

Lam 3:22 — "It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not."

Modern Corruption

No postmodern redefinition assails this title; the danger is severing mercy from holiness, as though God's pity required no atoning satisfaction.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The chief error touching the Father of mercies is not ideological but theological: to imagine a mercy that simply overlooks sin, a fatherly pity that needs no cross. Such sentimental mercy makes light of the holiness it must honor and empties the death of Christ of its necessity.

The principle to recover is that the mercy of the Father flows to sinners through the satisfaction of the Son, where mercy and truth meet together. The God who is "rich in mercy" is rich precisely because that mercy cost the blood of His own Son. The 1689 Confession confesses Him "most merciful" alongside "most holy and just"—the Father of mercies is no indulgent sentiment but the covenant compassion that pardons the guilty in Christ.

Hebrew Roots

The title joins fatherhood and compassion to name God as the wellspring of all mercy.

expand to see more

Greek patēr — father; here the source or originator, as "father of lights."

Greek oiktirmos — compassion, tender pity; the plural "mercies" of 2 Corinthians 1:3.

Hebrew raḥamīm — tender mercies, from the word for the womb; deep yearning pity.

Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast covenant love, often joined with mercy and compassion.

The plural "mercies" signals the manifold and inexhaustible compassions of God.

Usage

"Doctrinally, the title grounds the doctrine of God's mercy and the comfort of the afflicted saint."

"Pastorally, it directs the broken-hearted to a God whose compassions fail not."

"Liturgically, it opens many prayers and blessings as the address of the comfortless to their God."
